2610.37763.title: Hot off the Stacks: X-rays in Romulus25, Part I - Comparisons to Observations from eRosita

figures.caption: Figure 1.— Histograms of the two galaxy samples from Romulus25: Jarok [Left] and Rekar [Right] for comparisons with the observed eROSITA X-ray stacks of [12] and [75], respectively. Galaxy sample Rekar includes all of the isolated halos in R25 between log M∗ = 10.0 —11.5 M⊙ and is further subdivided into the following four mass bins [75]: 2$\times$M31-mass, M31-mass, MW-mass, and sub L∗ mass galaxies The galaxies in sample Jarok are a sub population of Rekar with stellar masses between M∗ = 10.2 —11.2 M⊙, and is split into two bins: High Mass and Low Mass as in [12].

Figure 2.— Images of three example galaxies across our stellar mass sample from R25 including a star forming galaxy with a strong disk at $M_{*}=1.2\times 10^{11}M_{\odot}$, a quenched galaxy at $M_{*}=7.1\times 10^{10}M_{\odot}$, and a flocculent star forming galaxy at $M_{*}=1.8\times 10^{10}M_{\odot}$. (Left) Gas density maps of each galaxy show the structure of the central gas disk or bulge of each galaxy and their inner gas halo. (Middle) RGB image of the galaxy’s stellar component covering the magnitude range 18 to 26 mag/arc2. (Right) Finally, we show a map of X-ray photon counts for each of our example galaxies for a simulated eROSITA observation at a distance of z - 0.01. While our example galaxies varying across stellar mass in size, shape, compactness, and structure, galaxies from R25 have been scaled to match the stellar mass-halo mass and black hole mass-stellar mass relations. They also fit the $M-\sigma$ and mass-metallicity scaling relations without further scaling.

Figure 3.— Comparisons between the Jarok R25 sample (pink) and the observed stacked X-ray surface brightness profiles from [12] (red and blue). The left column includes galaxies from the low stellar mass, log${}_{10}(M_{*}/M_{\odot}=10.2-10.7$, half of the simulated and observed galaxies, while the right column displays the profiles for the high stellar mass galaxies, log${}_{10}(M_{*}/M_{\odot})=10.7-11.2$. Upper and lower rows show our results splitting the sample between observed star forming (blue) and quiescent (red) galaxies, respectively. The pink horizontal error bars shows the bin size for the Jarok R25 sample, as in the observations.

Figure 4.— Direct comparisons between the star forming and quenched galaxies of the Jarok sample in the two low (Left) and high (Right) mass bins defined by [12]. Simulated quenched galaxy SB stacks are now shown in red (sSFR <1.6 M⊙ yr-1), while simulated star forming galaxy SB stacks are show in blue (sSFR >1.6 M⊙ yr-1). Horizontal error bars indicate the range of each stellar mass bin as in Figure 3.

Figure 5.— Comparisons between the Rekar R25 sample (pink) and the observed stacked X-ray surface brightness profiles from [75] (purple and green). The upper row includes galaxies from the two lower stellar mass sub-samples including log${}_{10}(M_{*}/M_{\odot})=10.0-10.5$ (Top Left) and log${}_{10}(M_{*}/M_{\odot})=10.5-11.0$ (Top Right). While the lower row includes surface brightness profiles from the two highest stellar mass sub-samples: log${}_{10}(M_{*}/M_{\odot})=11.0-11.25$ (Bottom Left) and log${}_{10}(M_{*}/M_{\odot})=11.25-11.5$ (Bottom Right).

Figure 6.— Galaxy halo total X-ray luminosity as a function of galaxy stellar mass. Galaxies from Rekar sample are shown in pink, with the solid line indicating the median Lχ for the simulated galaxies within 0.1 dex M∗ bins when we include both Brehmsstrahlung and metal line emission (See Section V.2). The pink shaded region indicates the standard deviation of R25 galaxies’ Lχ values. The dashed pink line indicates the mean Lχ only considering Brehmsstrahlung emission to account for potentially overabundant hot gas due to a lack of metal cooling in our simulations [For details see Section VII.1]. Purple and dark purple points are X-ray luminosities from observed galaxies with eROSITA [76, as in Figure 2] and yellow points are from [2]. Grey dotted, dashed, and dot dash lines indicate comparable measurements from EAGLE, TNG100, and SIMBA simulation groups. Before correcting for the lack of high temperature metal cooling in Romulus25, the Rekar sample galaxies are at least 0.5 dex higher than observations above a stellar mass of 1011 M⊙ and we see a much steeper relationship between Lχ and M∗ than [75]. However, between log(M∗) = 10.0 —11.0 M⊙, our mean Brehmsstrahlung-only Lχ values (dashed pink line) are much closer to matching observed measurements, though our scatter is much wider. Compared to other cosmological simulations, our Brehmsstrahlung-only Lχ values sit almost directly between between EAGLE and TNG at the X-ray brightest end and SIMBA at the dimmest in soft X-rays.

2610.37763.abstract: Recent observations from the from Spectrum Roentgen Gamma (SRG)/eROSITA all-sky survey data have helped to illuminate the hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) around galaxies at Milky Way-masses and above. In our study, we explore the hot X-ray emitting (T \textgreater 10$^6$ K) component of the CGM in over 750 galaxies from the Romulus25 cosmological simulation (Tremmel et al. 2017) between 10.0 < log(M$_*/M_{\odot}$) < 11.5. We forward-model soft X-ray [0.5 - 2.0] keV observations of our simulated galaxies using pyXSIM and SIXTE to measure the X-ray surface brightness (SB) profiles of the hot CGM. We then compare the average X-ray surface brightness profiles of six stellar-mass selected sub-samples to compare to the observational results from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al. 2024a. Broadly, we find that our stacked SB profiles are too bright compared to observations from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al.(2024a) particularly in the inner CGM. Additionally, we calculate the X-ray luminosity (L$_{\chi}$) of the hot CGM for each galaxy and compare the average L$_{\chi}$ across stellar mass to observations from Zhang et al. (2024b) as well as measurements from the EAGLE, TNG, SIMBA simulations. Across stellar mass, the average L$_{\chi}$ of galaxies from Romulus25 are brighter than observations except at the lower, Milky Way-mass end where we are in relative agreement with both observations and most other simulations. We also consider a zero-metallicity emission model, because Romulus25 does not have metal-line cooling, finding the average L$_{\chi}$ decreases by nearly an order-of-magnitude, which better matches observations particularly in the Milky Way-mass regime.

2610.37767.title: Resolving the thermal component of stellar feedback with the "anchor-and-refine" scheme in galactic simulations

figures.caption: Figure 2: Temporal evolution of a superbubble driven by a $10^{5}\,\rm M_{\odot}$ star cluster: ratio of thermal to total energy (top), physical radius (middle), and radial momentum (bottom). The blue and black solid lines represent the simulation results of the hybrid feedback and the "anchor-and-refine" scheme (both with mass resolution of 10 $\rm M_{\odot}$), the green dashed line denotes the classical analytical model (Weaver et al. 1977), and the orange shaded area indicates the range of results from the high-resolution 1D simulations in El-Badry et al. (2019), which depend on assumptions regarding mixing parameters.

Figure 4: Resolution dependence of superbubble properties driven by a $10^{5}\,\rm M_{\odot}$ star cluster for the hybrid feedback (blue) and the "anchor-and-refine" scheme (black). From top to bottom: ratio of thermal to total energy, physical radius, and radial momentum plotted against mass resolution. Symbols represent different evolutionary times: 5 Myr (triangles), 10 Myr (squares), and 15 Myr (circles).

Figure 5: Maps of basic properties of the isolated MW-mass galaxy run for the hybrid feedback (left) and the "anchor-and-refine" scheme (right). Top: face-on density map. Bottom: edge-on temperature map. All of the maps are shown at 0.54 Gyr with an extension of $40\times 40\,\rm kpc$.

Figure 6: X-ray maps of the isolated MW-mass galaxy run for the hybrid feedback (left) and the "anchor-and-refine" scheme (right). All of the maps are shown at 0.54 Gyr with an extension of $40\times 40\,\rm kpc$.

Bottom Panel: Burstiness of star formation rate, estimated as $\delta={\rm SFR-\langle SFR\rangle}$, where $\rm\langle SFR\rangle$ is the star formation history smoothed by a 0.1 Gyr window.

2610.37767.abstract: (abridged) Stellar feedback regulates galactic baryon cycles, but galaxy-scale simulations often cannot resolve supernova cooling radii. Momentum-based subgrid models can consequently underresolve the hot gas around young stars. We develop an "anchor-and-refine" feedback scheme that anchors a host cell near each star particle, preventing its displacement and preserving a thermal-feedback reservoir. When the cooling radius is resolved, all supernova energy is injected into the host cell as thermal energy; otherwise, the host cell is refined and terminal momentum is deposited into surrounding gas cells. Idealized tests agree with high-resolution simulations, yielding consistent superbubble properties and preserving hot interiors without artificial cooling. In an isolated Milky Way-mass galaxy, the scheme captures finer X-ray-emitting structures and a sharply defined, X-ray-bright central mid-plane. It also produces a smoother star formation history than pure hybrid feedback. Hot gas dominates outflow mass loading, with the mass-loading factor plateauing at approximately 0.2 at heights z>1 kpc. Phase decomposition indicates that hot gas sustains a steady, energy-driven wind, whereas cooler outflows decline with height because of radiative cooling and gravitational fallback. These results highlight the role of thermal feedback in driving galactic winds. By preserving hot superbubble interiors and the partition of thermal and kinetic energy, anchor-and-refine improves the treatment of hot gas, star formation, and feedback at limited resolution, supporting future applications to galaxy-scale and cosmological zoom-in simulations.

2610.37769.title: Extra! Extra! X-ray Emission!: X-rays in Romulus25, Part II - Physical Drivers of X-ray Emission in the CGM

figures.caption: Figure 1.— The black hole accretion and star formation histories for the PIONEER simulations. (Upper) The accretion history for the central SMBH for each of the four GM galaxies which includes two galaxies, R0 and GM1 (solid blue lines) which steadily accreted material into their SMBH until z = 0. The other two galaxies, GM2 and GM3 experience a peak in SMBH accretion at z $\sim$ 1, accrete steadily for 2 to 4 Gyr before having accretion fall steeply remain significantly low until z = 0. (Middle) The SFH of the same GM galaxies above with BHs. Here, we see that R0 and GM1 remain star forming through their evolution to z = 0, while GM2 and GM3 are fully quenched of star formation at z = 1 and remain passive through to z = 0. (Lower) The SFH for the four GM galaxies without BHs (dashed lines) all remain star forming throughout their evolution to z = 0.

Figure 2.— Total X-ray emissivity of each galaxy halo in the Rekar subsample (calculated via an APEC model as described in Section III) with continuum and metal line emission (Left) and only continuum emission (Right) as a function of total hot gas (T >105.5 K) in the CGM. Grey points on the right figure reproduce the metal line emission points from left figure. Points are colored by average metallicity of the hot gas in the CGM. Circles indicate all galaxies which include a SMBH at its center, triangles with white outlines do not have a central SMBH. We find that the strong trend between x-ray emissivity in the soft band [0.5-2 keV] and the total amount of hot gas is preserved with or without the inclusion of metal line emission, as is the secondary trend with metallicity.

Figure 3.— The X-ray surface brightness profile of the 8 PIONEER GM simulated galaxies. Galaxies with and without BHs are denoted by solid and dashed lines, respectively. The two galaxies that are brightest in the X-ray soft band are R0 and GM1 (solid blue lines), which a have CGM that are impacted by both AGN and stellar feedback. Next in brightness are R0noBH and GM1noBH (blue dashed lines) and then GM2noBH and GM3noBH (red/orange dashed lines) which all have CGM that only have energy injected into them by stellar feedback. Notably, R0noBH and GM1noBH have larger stellar masses resulting in larger energy injection and brighter $S_{\chi}$ profiles. Finally, the two galaxies with the dimmest X-ray surface brightness profiles are GM2 and GM3 which each have central SMBH but have been fully quenched of both stellar and SMBH feedback since z = 1.

Figure 4.— Profiles of the hot gas mass (T >105.5 K) in the CGM for all eight of the GM galaxies. Colors and linestyles as in Figure 3. We find a similar trend in this figure as we see when examining the X-ray surface brightness profiles (Figure 3). The galaxies that are the brightest in X-rays are the galaxies with the most hot gas mass in their CGM: P0 and GM1. Next in order of hot gas mass are the pairs, P0noBH and GM1noBH, and then, GM2noBH and Gm3noBH. Finally, the galaxies with the least amount of hot gas mass (and similarly the least X-ray emission) are GM2 and GM3, the only two quenched galaxies at z=0.

Figure 5.— Total energy injection from both SMBH feedback and stellar feedback in all of the 8 GM galaxies. Colors and linestyles as in Figure 3. At z = 0, the galaxies with the most total energy injection from both stars and the SMBH are R0 and GM1, the same galaxies that are also brightest in X-ray surface brightness. Next in terms of total energy injection are the galaxies with no black hole physics, approximately in order of stellar mass which correlates to stellar feedback. Lastly, as in X-ray surface brightness, GM2 and GM3 have the least energy injection having been quenched at z $\sim$ 1. By comparing this figure with Figure 4, we can directly tie the total energy injected by AGN and stellar feedback to the presence of hot gas mass in the CGM and in turn the X-ray SB.

Figure 6.— The profiles of gas density (Upper), temperature (Middle), and electron density (Lower) for the CGM of the eight GM galaxies. Line styles and colors as in Figure 3. Unlike in the profiles of X-ray SB and hot gas mass, the profiles of temperature, gas density, and electron density do not show the same trends as the previous figures and the measurements in each set of profiles are much more consistent. There are slight deviations: for example, the inner CGM temperature of the two quenched galaxies GM2 and GM3 is a bit lower than the rest which are all star forming. There are also a few discrete peaks in the density profiles at varying distances in the CGM due to the presence of dwarf galaxy satellites. However, none of these properties are significantly distinct enough to explain the differences in X-ray brightness in the GM galaxy sample.

Figure 7.— Metallicity profiles for the eight GM galaxy CGM. Colors and linestyles as in Figure 3. There is a distinct bimodality shown in this figure between the galaxies with BHs (solid lines) which all have similarly high metallicities and those without BHs (dashed lines) which all have roughly an order of magnitude lower metallcity. One exception is GM2noBH which has a slightly higher metallicity profile beyond about 120 kpc. This difference is likely due to metal enrichment from dwarf galaxies in the outer CGM, which also explains the small bump in the metallicity profile of GM3noBH at $\sim$ 70 kpc. In addition to the presence of hot gas mass in the CGM, the difference in the metallicities of these galaxies with and without black holes also appears to play a significant role in setting the X-ray brightness of their CGM.

Figure 8.— (Left:) Soft band X-ray emissivity for the galaxies from the Romulus25 Rekar sample introduced in Paper I as a function of the hot gas mass in their CGM. Points are colored by the average hot gas mass metallicity and individual galaxies have been hand-selected (white dots) and labeled (numbers 1 through 7) for further exploration in the right panel. There is a strong linear trend between the soft X-ray emission and total hot gas mass in the CGM and a secondary trend with the metallicity of the hot gas. (Right:) Average overall temperature of the hot gas, log(T/K) ¿ 5.5), as a function of hot gas mass as in the left panel. Unlike in the GM case, in the Romulus25 sample, galaxies with metal-rich CGM are also hotter as a result of the feedback energy both heating gas and moving metals of out the disk.

Figure 9.— Soft X-ray spectrum for the hand-selected galaxies shown in Figure 8. Galaxies with higher average metallicity CGM are also hotter and tend to have higher and flatter emission spectra, while galaxies with less hot gas mass have steeper emission spectra and are not emitting as much X-ray energy.

2610.37769.abstract: Characterizing the hot (T ~ 10$^{6}$ K) circumgalactic medium (CGM) around Milky Way-mass (MW-mass) galaxies is critical to a full understanding of galaxy evolution. In this second paper of the "X-rays in Romulus25" series, we unpack the specific physical processes giving rise to the presence of hot X-ray emitting gas in the halos of galaxies from the Romulus25 (R25) simulation, focusing on L$_{*}$ galaxies. We determine that a strong correlation appears between the mass of hot CGM gas, M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$, and the X-ray emissivity, $\epsilon_{\chi}$, measured in the first paper of this series, (Sanchez et al. 2026a, submitted). There is also a secondary correlation between M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$ and $\epsilon_{\chi}$ with the average metallicity of the hot CGM gas, $\bar{Z}_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$. We use the well-studied PIONEER simulations from Sanchez et al. (2019), a set of zoom-in MW-mass galaxies run with the genetic modification technique of Roth et al. (2016) and the same physics as R25, to interpret these correlations. We determine that the presence of hot X-ray emitting gas is determined by two key processes: 1) the quantity of hot gas mass in the CGM, M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$, is set by the combined total energy injection of $both$ stellar and AGN feedback, and 2) together the average temperature and metallicity of the hot CGM changes the soft X-ray spectrum of the gas resulting in brighter metal-rich CGM and dimmer metal-poor CGM for the same quantity of M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$. These results indicate, for the first time, that metal-rich gas halos may bias X-ray observations of MW-mass galaxies.

2610.37774.abstract: Context: Massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) are traditionally considered "red-and-dead" based on optical observations. However, ultraviolet (UV) spectroscopy can uncover a hidden population of young stars with a sub-one-per cent mass fraction. Aims: We measure the young stellar mass fraction in NGC 3115, a massive isolated lenticular galaxy, to test the ubiquity and spatial distribution of this component beyond previously studied ellipticals. Methods: Using SOAR/Goodman spectra and line-strength fitting, we modelled the star-formation history with a single bulk stellar population plus a young component (constant star-formation over the last 1 Gyr). We used ultranest to derive posterior distributions for age, metallicity, [Mg/Fe], and the young stellar mass fraction. Results: By tracking spatial variations in U-band indices, we found the young stellar mass fraction peaks at $0.69^{+0.09}_{-0.15}\%$ in the centre, dropping to zero beyond 1 kpc. This young component correlates with kinematic structures, dominating in the pressure-supported region. We interpret this as residual central star formation fueled by internal processes, such as recycled stellar material. Alternative UV-bright models (e.g., extreme horizontal branch stars) yielded poorer fits and unphysically high mass fractions. Conclusions: Young stars in old, "red-and-dead" galaxies are more common than expected. Their presence across various ETGs with similar gradients indicates that residual star formation is a ubiquitous feature, offering key constraints on the baryon cycle in these galaxies.

2610.37775.title: Ejected and Rejected: Strong Scatterings in Dense Star Clusters

figures.caption: Figure 1: Kick boundary for strong scatterings for $M=M_{\rm s}$ (Eq. 9). The darker colors correspond to slower velocities, ranging from $$v=0$$ to $v=v_{\mathrm{esc}}$. We have mirrored $\Delta v_{\perp}$ for visualization purposes, although by definition $\Delta v_{\perp}>0$. The kick boundary is symmetric for v=0 (reflecting the isotropy of field star velocities) but becomes increasingly biased towards $\Delta v_{||}$ as $v\to v_{\rm esc}$: the test star experiences a headwind of field stars in this limit, and preferentially slows down.

Figure 2: The differential rate distribution, ${\rm d}^{2}\Gamma/{\rm d}\Delta v_{\parallel}{\rm d}\Delta v_{\perp}$, for an object in a Keplerian orbit around an $M_{\bullet}=10^{6}\,M_{\odot}$ central object. Here, $\gamma=7/4$, $a=0.1\,\mathrm{pc}$, and the eccentricity $e=0.99$. The scatterers and test object have the same mass $M=M_{\rm s}=1\,M_{\odot}$. Each panel depicts a different snapshot along the orbit of the test particle, moving from pericenter (left panel) to apocenter (right panel). The colored frames of each panel correspond to the equivalently colored point along the example orbit in the bottom panel. The color shading in each panel corresponds to the log value of ${\rm d}^{2}\Gamma/({\rm d}\Delta v_{||}{\rm d}\Delta v_{\perp})$, multiplied by $|\Delta v_{||}\Delta v_{\perp}|$ to have units of rate (yr-1).

In this case, $r_{\mathrm{inf}}$ is set by a background stellar density profile of $\gamma=7/4$.

Figur$e$ 8: Plots showing different ejection regimes in the sp$$a$$ce of semimajor axis a and eccentricity e, for black hole masses of $10^{6}\,M_{\odot}$ (top panel), $10^{5}\,M_{\odot}$ (middle panel), and $10^{4}\,M_{\odot}$ (bottom panel). All systems take $M=M_{\rm s}=1\,M_{\odot}$. Solid lines show $\Delta E_{c,\max}=E$ for different values of $\gamma$ (color-coded as per the inset key). Regions to the left of these solid lines are in the saturated kick regime. The dashed lines indicate where $t_{E}=P$ for each system of the same color; regions left of these are in the diffusively saturated kick regime. Saturation of ejections via strong scatterings becomes important for small $M_{\bullet}$, large a, and large $\gamma$. The hatched region is where $r_{p}\leq 8R_{g}$, with $R_{g}=GM_{\bullet}/c^{2}$, a typical minimum pericenter to avoid a plunge. The dotted line notates the $r_{\mathrm{inf}}$ corresponding to $\gamma=7/4$.

2610.37775.abstract: Understanding the evolution of collisional stellar systems is key to predicting both the bulk evolution of dense star clusters and also the rates of tidal disruption events, extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), stellar ejections, and other loss cone phenomena. Although a majority of the evolution is dictated by weak, small-angle scatterings, rare close encounters resulting in strong scatterings can sometimes produce qualitatively different outcomes. To systematically determine the astrophysical importance of strong scatterings, we derive the exact differential rate distribution of velocity kicks in isotropic and spherically symmetric distribution functions representing globular and nuclear star clusters, while also deriving the distribution boundaries and approximate rate scalings. We then extend this formalism to derive approximate rates of energy and angular momentum kicks for objects in the nuclear star cluster, and then apply this framework to study (i) ejections and (ii) ``cancellation'' of extreme mass ratio inspirals. We find that ejection rates are complicated in some regimes due to the saturation of the strong kick distribution and the breakdown of the weak limit, likely enhancing the effect of loss cone shielding. We also determine that a sizable fraction of proto-EMRIs will likely be canceled by strong scatterings, highlighting the need for future work to determine to what degree strong scatterings impact the true EMRI rate.

2610.37821.abstract: Direct detections of dust in typical $z>8$ galaxies remain untenable, despite the presence of dust suggested by rest-frame UV/optical spectro-photometry. Informed by cosmological zoom-in simulations where dust particles evolve on-the-fly, we present a novel method for inferring dust masses in high-redshift galaxies using stellar half-light radii and UV/optical attenuation. Our methods reproduce observed trends at lower redshift, ultimately diverging from Milky Way-based calibration factors by up to $\sim1.5$ dex. We apply this method to observed JWST galaxies from $6<z<14$, and find dust masses in the range $M_{\rm dust}\sim10^3-10^5\,M_\odot$ that are fully consistent with upper limits from ALMA, and suggest an early dust enrichment period by supernovae followed by efficient grain destruction in the hot gas. Future observations may use our tabulated calibration to infer dust masses over a wide range of stellar masses and redshifts.

2610.37971.abstract: We introduce a new, independent modeling component to the Carousel Lens series by exploiting the spatially-resolved kinematics contained within the lensed arcs, which so far has remained rather underexplored in strong-lensing analyses. We present an end-to-end forward-modeling framework that reconstructs an integral-field spectroscopic datacube from a parameterization of the lens convergence profile together with the line-of-sight velocity, velocity dispersion, and surface brightness profiles of the unlensed source. The kinematic structure of the source acts as an additional set of ray-traceable markers distributed across every lensed image, inaccessible from imaging data alone. Furthermore, by generating an [OII] emission-line datacube, we isolate a single source redshift and remove lens and line-of-sight light contamination. We apply this framework to deep VLT/MUSE observations of the Carousel Lens, modeling the [OII] emission of the quadruply-imaged star-forming galaxy at $z_{\rm s} = 1.432$ that anchors the system's cosmography constraints. We measure an Einstein radius $\theta_{\rm E} = 12.816''^{+0.005}_{-0.007}$ and a logarithmic slope $\gamma = 1.412^{+0.002}_{-0.002}$, tightening the statistical uncertainties on both by roughly a factor of $2-2.5$ relative to the corresponding flat emission-line map model. We find that the source galaxy exhibits a strong rotation, lies confidently along the star-forming main sequence, and has an inferred central black hole mass of $\log M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot} = 7.89 \pm 0.51$. These results establish datacube-level forward modeling as a practical and independent route to traditional image-based lens models in the current systematics-limited regime, and one that extends naturally to this system's other lensed sources and to other lens systems.

2610.38035.abstract: Stellar shells-concentric arc-like tidal features formed in galaxy mergers-provide a valuable record of recent galaxy assembly histories encoding both the merger event and the gravitational potential of the host galaxy. We compare shell systems in observations and cosmological simulations from two complementary perspectives. First, we show that simulations predict a substantial population of very large (>100kpc) shells that are rarely observed, revealing a potentially important discrepancy between simulations and reality. Because the scales of observed and simulated shell systems differ significantly, we focus on a comparison of merger histories. Using a shell-identification method, we estimate merger times for a sample of nearby massive prolate rotators and compare them with merger histories derived from cosmological simulations. We also present ongoing efforts to expand the sample of deeply imaged prolate rotators using observations from the Milankovic telescope, paving the way for future studies based on larger observational samples.

2610.38159.abstract: Using the exus\ N-body/hydrodynamic framework, we show that stellar bars that emerge in high-redshift disc galaxies are different in their orbital characteristics compared to their low-redshift counterparts. We identify bar-supporting orbits and, among them, find the fraction of chaotic orbits compared to regular orbits ($f_{\rm chaos}$). This fraction rises above 60\% for models with $f_{\rm gas} > 60 \%$; for $f_{\rm gas} \lesssim 60\%$, we observe chaotic fractions close to zero. The emerging bars seen in the $f_{\rm gas}= 80\%$ and $100\%$ simulations collapse in $\lesssim$1 Gyr to form central bulges supported by rotation, and this collapse follows soon after the chaotic fraction starts to dominate ($f_{\rm chaos} \gtrsim 50\%)$. Moreover, the gravitational potential in those simulations steepens rapidly over that period, and by integrating the chaotic orbits, we find that orbits that deviate from the evolving mean field are more likely to be chaotic. Hence, we argue that the irregularity associated with the rapidly evolving, central potentials drives higher chaotic fractions in these gas-rich bars. As a result, the emergent bars collapse through `violent relaxation' to form oblate rotating bulges. Supporting evidence for this picture comes from the fact that particles of different mass share identical radial profiles, a natural consequence of the rapid relaxation process.

2610.38192.abstract: We present near-infrared K-band ($1.94$--$2.52~\mu$m) spectroscopy of the deeply embedded protostellar source HOPS\,370, obtained with the TIFR--ARIES Near Infrared Spectrometer (TANSPEC) on the 3.6-m Devasthal Optical Telescope (DOT). The spectrum is dominated by prominent molecular hydrogen ($\rm H_2$) ro-vibrational emission, with multiple transitions detected from the $1$--$0$ S, $2$--$1$ S, and $1$--$0$ Q branches. Using the intrinsically linked $\rm H_2$ $1$--$0$ Q(3) and $1$--$0$ S(1) transitions, which arise from the same upper energy level, we derive a visual extinction of $A_V = 23.24 \pm 1.25$ mag, corresponding to $A_K = 2.50 \pm 0.13$ mag, consistent with the embedded Class~0/I nature of the source. The diagnostic line ratio $F(2$--$1~{\rm S}(1))/F(1$--$0~{\rm S}(1)) = 0.12 \pm 0.01$ is consistent with thermal excitation and disfavors ultraviolet fluorescence as the dominant excitation mechanism. Assuming optically thin emission and local thermodynamic equilibrium, we derive an $\rm H_2$ excitation diagram that yields an excitation temperature of $2078 \pm 215$ K and a molecular hydrogen column density of $(1.93 \pm 0.93)\times10^{20}$ cm$^{-2}$. We further derive an ortho-to-para ratio of $2.45 \pm 0.21$, indicating substantial shock-driven thermal processing while remaining below the high-temperature equilibrium value of 3. Taken together, these diagnostics indicate that the molecular hydrogen emission in HOPS\,370 originates predominantly in warm, shock-heated gas most likely associated with its protostellar outflow. Our results demonstrate the diagnostic power of combined S- and Q-branch $\rm H_2$ spectroscopy for constraining the physical conditions and excitation history of deeply embedded protostellar systems.

2610.38235.abstract: Determining how the Milky Way warp evolves provides constraints on the formation and dynamical evolution of galactic disks. Using Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment Data Release 19 (APOGEE DR19) spectroscopy, we estimate ages for 222,355 red giants. With Gaia astrometry and geometric distances, we analyze 168,824 of these stars in five age bins spanning $0$--$10$ Gyr. The warp-related radial vertical-velocity ($V_Z$) profile of young red giants ($0$--$2$ Gyr) is broadly consistent with those of classical Cepheids and young open clusters. Over $9\leq R<12$ kpc, we find that the mean $V_Z$ values of the intermediate-age red giants ($2$--$4$ and $4$--$6$ Gyr) are $1.48\pm0.46$ and $1.49\pm0.52$ km s$^{-1}$ higher than that of the young population, respectively. By contrast, at $R\simeq12$--$13$ kpc, the $V_Z$ profiles of the $0$--$6$ Gyr red giants are consistent within their uncertainties. The intermediate-age enhancement persists across our robustness tests and may reflect smaller effective kinematic warp onset radii for the intermediate-age populations. The observed velocity differences may arise from the combined effects of earlier perturbations and the present-day warp, or from differences in vertical structure among stellar populations.

2610.38490.title: The Influence of Hubble Expansion on the Future Merger of the Milky Way and Andromeda

The value $+\infty$ indicates that the MW and M31 do not merge in the $\Lambda$CDM simulation of that cell. 2610.38490.abstract: Most existing idealized simulations of galaxy mergers neglect Hubble expansion, as the local Hubble flow is curved by overdensities and the expansion effect is weak at these scales. However, even in the gravity-dominated Local Group (LG), the expansion itself still persists, and it has been shown important in some LG-related studies. Here we take the future merger of the Milky Way (MW) and Andromeda (M31) as a case study to investigate the differences between simulations with and without Hubble expansion. We perform a suite of idealized N-body simulations of the MW--M31 system under pure Newtonian, $\Lambda$CDM, and $w_0w_a$CDM scenarios, testing different masses and proper motions of galaxies informed by current observational constraints. At low M31 tangential velocities, especially in cases where the two galaxies merge within a Hubble time, the expansion effect is negligible; while at high velocities (>66.5 km/s), the $\Lambda$CDM simulations introduce a noticeable delay in the merger time compared to the Newtonian ones and may even alter the final fate of the system, but the caveat here is that the isolated-pair idealization and the assumed expansion history break down. The delay is also present but less pronounced in the $w_0w_a$CDM runs. When M33 and the Large Magellanic Cloud are included, the differences in merger times are reduced. In summary, Hubble expansion can play a noticeable role for galaxy mergers with high tangential velocities, but its actual influence on the MW--M31 merger depends on the precise masses and proper motions to be determined in the future.

2610.38589.abstract: We aim to improve and extend the imaging capabilities of the GRAVITY beam combiner instrument of ESOs VLTI with respect to reconstruction software in the Galactic Center. We revise and develop the image reconstruction code GRAVITY-RESOLVE $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$, which has been specifically developed to reconstruct stars in the Galactic Center with GRAVITY. The main objectives are to increase the limiting magnitude in GRAVITY images, reduce its computational runtime, and allow for a joint reconstruction of multiple, spatially separate datasets/pointings on sky. We apply $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ to recent GRAVITY data, featuring the implemented GRAVITY-faint mode as part of GRAVITY+, the upgrade of GRAVITY. We reconstruct visibility phases and amplitudes and present the first GRAVITY image reconstructed with $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ from these quantities. We demonstrate NIR mosaicking with $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ by jointly reconstructing nine separately acquired datasets of 2025 into a single image on a scale of $\simeq 3390\ \text{AU}\times 3390\ \text{AU}$, corresponding to $409.6\ \text{mas}\times 409.6\ \text{mas}$. With dedicated injection tests of point sources into GRAVITY data, we estimate the limiting magnitude to be $m_{\text{K}}\ \simeq\ 20.0$ within a radius of $25\ \text{mas}$ around the field center when reconstructing from closure phases and visibility amplitudes. We report on the discovery of two new faint stars in the Galactic Center: S303 and S304. Finally, we find a decrease in computational runtime by a factor of at least $\sim10$. With $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$, we demonstrate GRAVITYs capabilities for NIR imaging. We show that $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ is a fast, precise, and deep image reconstruction tool for Galactic Center observations, enabling the discovery of even more faint stars.

2610.38607.title: The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front

2610.38607.abstract: The Milky Way is commonly depicted as having four major spiral arms, including the Norma-Outer arm, and a central stellar bar whose properties remain debated. Masers associated with young high-mass stars have been used to trace a segment of the "Norma arm" extending from one end of the Galaxy's central stellar bar. Recent work suggests that these masers may reside along a spiral arm or occupy the dominant x1 stellar orbits that give the bar its shape. We now use a new generation of N-body, hydrodynamic simulations to argue that these million-year old masers instead trace the Galactic bar's Quadrant I shock front or, equivalently, its dust lane. This implies that the bar dust-lane is star-forming, shedding new light on our understanding of star formation processes in the Milky Way. By associating the masers with the simulated shock front, we determine the bar's parameters to be: a ~ 4.3 +/- 0.2 kpc, b ~ 2.3 +/- 0.2 kpc, phi = 20 (+5/-2) deg, Omega_p <~ 40 km s^-1 kpc^-1, representing the bar's semi-major and semi-minor half-lengths, inclination angle and pattern speed, respectively. This raises questions about the Milky Way's spiral structure and suggests that the Galactic bar is long, slow and star-forming.

2610.38633.abstract: The nature of spiral arms in galaxies remains debated, with several competing formation scenarios, including density waves, kinematic spirals, dynamic spirals, and recurrent modes, that are difficult to distinguish observationally. We tested two kinematic methods - the phase reversal method and the velocity harmonic dominance method - using toy models and mock data from TNG50 simulations. For bar resonances, the phase reversal method is strongly orientation-dependent and yields reliable corotation estimates only when the bar is aligned with the disc minor axis. For spiral arms, the phase reversal method does not always yield reliable results and should be used in tondem with another kinematic method. The velocity harmonic dominance method is more robust: it distinguishes between density wave, kinematic, and dynamic spiral patterns, although it still shows some sensitivity to orientation. Uncertainties in the rotation curve do not strongly affect its results. We also apply both methods to the observed grand-design spiral galaxy NGC3938 as an illustrative example; the results suggest the presence of multiple spiral modes, consistent with the recurrent modes scenario and this interpretation relies on different indirect evidence. Based on our findings, we propose a strategy for classifying spiral structure in observed galaxies that combines multiple independent tests. Applying this analysis to an extended sample will allow us to validate its predictive power and to investigate the diversity of spiral formation scenarios.

2610.38654.abstract: We present a detailed study of the open cluster Berkeley 31 using Gaia DR3 astrometry, Gaia-ESO Survey DR5.1 spectroscopy, and multi-wavelength photometry. We identify 329 probable cluster members from their proper motions and trigonometric parallaxes and use them to examine the cluster's fundamental parameters, stellar populations, and Galactic orbit. The cluster is located at a distance of $6024 \pm 181$ pc, with a color excess of $E(B-V)=0.148 \pm 0.047$ mag, and has a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] $=-0.36 \pm 0.04$ dex and $\langle [\alpha/{\rm Fe}] \rangle=0.21 \pm 0.04$ dex. Isochrone fitting gives an age of $3.7 \pm 0.2$ Gyr, consistent with the independent chemical-clock estimate of $3.72 \pm 1.42$ Gyr. The systemic radial velocity is $57.89 \pm 0.08$ km s$^{-1}$. We find that about 38% of the MS stars are unresolved binary candidates with $q \gtrsim 0.5$. We identify 62 BSSs and 2 YSS candidates, including 48 BSSs and both YSSs not previously reported in the literature. We constructed multi-wavelength SEDs for these stars, including Swift/UVOT data for 28 BSSs. Two BSSs show clear ultraviolet excesses and are consistent with compact hot companions, one with a hot WD and the other with a pre-ELM WD. The present orbital parameters give a guiding radius of $12.29 \pm 0.29$ kpc and an eccentricity of $0.11 \pm 0.01$. Comparison with the estimated chemical birth radius indicates a moderate outward shift of the guiding center, with the present orbital position also contributing to the radial displacement. These results consistently describe Berkeley 31 as an intermediate-age, metal-poor outer-disk cluster and place its stellar populations in the context of its Galactic dynamical history.

2610.38699.title: On The Scaling Relations Between Black Holes And The Galaxy/Bulge Mass And Their Connections With The Black Hole Occupation Fraction

figures.caption: Figure 1: Black hole–host galaxy scaling relations predicted by FEGA25 at $z=0$. The left panel shows $M_{\rm BH}$ as a function of total stellar mass, while the right panel shows the relation with bulge mass. Black solid curves indicate the median relations obtained without imposing a black hole mass cut, with black dashed curves enclosing the 16th–84th percentile range. Blue circles and orange squares show the median relations obtained after selecting black holes with $M_{\rm BH}>10^{5}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$ and $M_{\rm BH}>10^{6}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, respectively, while the corresponding dotted contours enclose the $2\sigma$ regions of the selected distributions. The horizontal dashed line marks $M_{\rm BH}=10^{5}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$. The vertical dashed lines indicate $\log(M_{\star}/{\rm M}_{\odot})=9.5$ in the left panel and $\log(M_{\rm bulge}/{\rm M}_{\odot})=7$ in the right panel. The comparison illustrates how imposing a black hole mass threshold preferentially affects the low-mass regime, whereas the selected and no-cut relations progressively converge toward higher host masses.

Figure 2: Black hole mass as a function of total stellar mass predicted by FEGA25 at $z=0$, separated according to galaxy morphology, characterized by the bulge-to-total stellar mass ratio ($B/T$). The first three panels show the relations for the three morphological classes, while the fourth panel provides a direct comparison among them. Black solid curves indicate the median relations obtained without imposing a black hole mass cut, with black dashed curves enclosing the corresponding 16th–84th percentile ranges. Blue solid curves show the median relations for galaxies hosting black holes with $M_{\rm BH}>10^{5}\,M_{\odot}$, while blue dashed and dotted curves indicate the corresponding $1\sigma$ and $2\sigma$ regions, respectively.

Figure 3: Evolution of the $M_{\rm BH}$–$M_{\star}$ relation predicted by FEGA25 and comparison with the hydrodynamical zoom-in simulation NewCluster. The black solid line shows the median relation predicted by FEGA25 at $$z=0$$ and is repeated in all panels as a reference. At $z=1$, 2, and 3, the colored solid lines with open circles show the corresponding FEGA25 median relations, while the associated contours enclose the $1\sigma$ and $2\sigma$ regions. Dark-gray points show individual galaxies from NewCluster; the solid line with open squares indicates their median relation, and the dashed lines show the 16th and 84th percentiles. In the first panel, the FEGA25 prediction at z=0 is compared with NewCluster at $z=0.4$, the lowest redshift available for the hydrodynamical simulation. Only BHs with $M_{\rm BH}\geq 10^{5}\,M_{\odot}$ are considered. Contours extending below this BH mass limit are displayed at $\log(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot})=5$.

Figure 4:  Evolution of the $M_{\rm BH}$–$M_{\rm bulge}$ relation predicted by FEGA25 and comparison with the hydrodynamical zoom-in simulation NewCluster. The black solid line shows the median relation predicted by FEGA25 at $$z=0$$ and is repeated in all panels as a reference. At $z=1$, 2, and 3, the colored solid lines with open circles show the corresponding FEGA25 median relations, while the associated contours enclose the $1\sigma$ and $2\sigma$ regions. Dark-gray points show individual galaxies from NewCluster; the solid line with open squares indicates their median relation, and the dashed lines show the 16th and 84th percentiles. In the first panel, the FEGA25 prediction at z=0 is compared with NewCluster at $z=0.4$. Only BHs with $M_{\rm BH}\geq 10^{5}\,M_{\odot}$ are considered. Contours extending below this BH mass limit are displayed at $\log(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot})=5$.

Figure 5: Connection between black hole–host scaling relations and black hole occupation fractions predicted by FEGA25 at $z=0$. The upper panels show $M_{\rm BH}$ as a function of total stellar mass (left) and bulge stellar mass (right), while the lower panels show the corresponding black hole occupation fractions, $f_{\rm BH,occ}$. Blue circles and orange squares refer to the selections $M_{\rm BH}>10^{5}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$ and $M_{\rm BH}>10^{6}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, respectively, while the black curves in the upper panels show the no-cut relations. The vertical dashed lines mark the host masses at which $f_{\rm BH,occ}=0.5$, determined by interpolation between adjacent mass bins. For the stellar-mass relation, these occur at $\log(M_{\star,50}/{\rm M}_{\odot})\simeq 8.30$ and $9.19$ for the $10^{5}$ and $10^{6}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$ thresholds, respectively. For the bulge-mass relation, the $10^{6}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$ threshold reaches $f_{\rm BH,occ}=0.5$ at $\log(M_{{\rm bulge},50}/{\rm M}_{\odot})\simeq 7.88$, whereas the occupation fraction for $M_{\rm BH}>10^{5}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$ is already above 0.5 at the lower edge of the plotted bulge-mass range. The figure shows that large differences in occupation fraction do not necessarily translate into equally large differences in the corresponding median scaling relations, highlighting the complementary information carried by black hole demographics and black hole–host scaling relations.

Figure 6: Selection-induced offset in the black hole–host scaling relations as a function of the black hole occupation fraction predicted by FEGA25. The four panels show the results at $z=0$, 1, 2, and 3. The vertical axis is defined as $\Delta_{\rm sel}={\rm median}(\log M_{\rm BH})_{\rm cut}-{\rm median}(\log M_{\rm BH})_{\rm no\,cut}$ and therefore quantifies, in each host-mass bin, the upward shift of the median scaling relation induced by the adopted black hole mass threshold. Blue and orange curves correspond to $M_{\rm BH}>10^{5}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$ and $M_{\rm BH}>10^{6}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, respectively. Solid curves with open circles show the results obtained when binning galaxies by total stellar mass, while dashed curves with open diamonds refer to bulge stellar mass. The vertical dashed line marks $f_{\rm BH,occ}=0.5$, and the horizontal dashed line indicates $\Delta_{\rm sel}=0$. Large values of $\Delta_{\rm sel}$ are preferentially associated with low occupation fractions, where the black hole mass cut selects only the high-$M_{\rm BH}$ tail of the underlying population. As $f_{\rm BH,occ}$ approaches unity, the selected and no-cut median relations progressively converge and $\Delta_{\rm sel}$ approaches zero. At fixed $f_{\rm BH,occ}$, however, the offset can differ substantially between the stellar-mass and bulge-mass relations, showing that the occupation fraction alone does not uniquely determine the selection bias and that its impact also depends on the host property used to define the scaling relation.

Figure 7: Comparison between the black hole–host galaxy scaling relations predicted by FEGA25 at $z=0$ and local observational samples. The left panel shows black hole mass as a function of bulge stellar mass, while the right panel shows the relation with total stellar mass. The FEGA25 predictions are obtained by selecting black holes with $M_{\rm BH}>10^{5}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$. Black solid curves show the median relations, black dashed curves indicate the 16th–84th percentile range, and black dash-dotted and dotted contours enclose the $1\sigma$ and $2\sigma$ regions, respectively. The density contours are restricted to $\log(M_{\rm BH}/{\rm M}_{\odot})\geq 5$. Blue solid curves show the best-fitting relations derived by Bentz and Manne-Nicholas [6], with the corresponding $\pm 1\sigma$ regions indicated by the blue shaded areas and dashed boundaries. Blue open diamonds show the individual measurements from Bentz and Manne-Nicholas [6]. Magenta open squares in the left panel show the bulge-mass measurements from Sturm and Reines [87], while orange crosses in the right panel show the total stellar-mass measurements from Reines and Volonteri [69]. The comparison illustrates the agreement between the FEGA25 predictions and the observed local black hole–host galaxy relations over the mass range probed by the data, while highlighting the substantial scatter toward lower host masses.

2610.38699.abstract: We investigate the black hole (BH)--host galaxy scaling relations predicted by the semianalytic model \texttt{FEGA25}, focusing on their dependence on BH mass threshold, galaxy morphology, and redshift, and on their connection with the BH occupation fraction (BHOF). Using the YS200 cosmological simulation as our reference volume, we study the $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\star}$ and $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\rm bulge}$ relations for different BH mass selections and compare their redshift evolution with the hydrodynamical zoom-in simulation \texttt{NewCluster}. We find that BH mass cuts primarily affect the low-mass regime, while the selected relations progressively converge toward the intrinsic no-cut relations at higher host masses. The $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\star}$ relation also depends systematically on galaxy morphology, with increasingly bulge-dominated systems preferentially occupying higher stellar masses. Over $z=0$--$3$, FEGA25 shows no clear systematic evolution of either scaling relation, consistent with a broadly preserved statistical connection between BH and host-galaxy growth. NewCluster shows no clear monotonic evolution either, although it exhibits larger scatter, particularly toward high host masses. We further show that BHOF and BH--host scaling relations encode complementary information. A low BHOF generally corresponds to a stronger selection-induced offset, but the mapping is not unique: substantially different occupation fractions can yield similar median scaling relations, and at fixed BHOF the bias depends on the host property and underlying BH mass distribution. At $z=0$, \texttt{FEGA25} is consistent with available observational constraints for both stellar- and bulge-mass relations, while predicting increased scatter and bending toward lower host masses.

2610.38767.title: The coupled evolution of nuclear star clusters and intermediate-mass black holes in a dwarf-galaxy merger

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the evolution of the fiducial merger simulation 1e3-NSC at (a) the time of first approach, (b) the starburst triggered by the galaxy interaction, (c) the post-starburst phase during which the BHs and NSCs are still unbound, (d) the NSC coalescence and BH binary formation, and (e) the BH merger phase. The first and second columns show the gas and stellar surface densities on galactic scales (scale bar: $1000\,\rm pc$), showing the full extent of both interacting galactic discs. To guide the eye, we over-plot the stellar surface density of new stars with the pre-existing NSCs in yellow/red. The third and fourth columns show gas and stellar surface densities zoomed in on the region around BH-1 (scale bar: $100\,\rm pc$). The trajectories of the two black holes are shown in black and white, respectively. Zoom-ins on the region around the BH show the gas supply (panels b and c, column 3) and the stellar environment of the BH (column 4). The evolution of the BH separation is shown as an inset in the third column of rows (d), at binary formation, and (e), shortly before the merger.

Figure 2: Evolution of the four merger simulations in comparison to the isolated simulation. The global star formation rate (SFR; panel a) shows a starburst between $150$–$300\,\rm Myr$ that is independent of the presence of an NSC or IMBH. The isolated simulation (grey) maintains a constant star formation rate, more than one order of magnitude below the SFR in the post-starburst phase.
Panel (b) shows the radial distance between the BHs, which also traces the distance between the NSCs (BHs always stay within $\lesssim 0.05$ pc from the NSC centre before NSC coalescence). In the fiducial simulation 1e3-NSC (blue), orbital decay due to dynamical friction leads to NSC coalescence at around $500\,\rm Myr$ (blue shaded area). After NSC coalescence, mass segregation leads to the formation of a BH binary and stellar scattering takes over until gravitational waves cause the BHs to merge at ${\sim}848\,\rm Myr$. BHs without an NSC but with the mass of the fiducial NSC–BH system, $10^{6}\,\rm M_{\odot}$ (orange), initially sink faster, but then form a binary that stalls at parsec scale, with an insufficient supply of stars for stellar scattering to facilitate a fast merger. Light IMBHs without an NSC ($10^{3}\,\rm M_{\odot}$,green; $10^{4}\,\rm M_{\odot}$ purple) show very slow sinking, with their apocentric distance still at $\gtrsim 50\,\rm pc$ at the end of the simulation. Panel (c) shows the individual masses of BH-1 and BH-2, which are indistinguishable visually in the simulations without NSC. The IMBH in the isolated galaxy (grey) grows much less than the same IMBH in the merger simulation.

Figure 3: Evolution of the two black holes (BH-1, BH-2) in the fiducial simulation 1e3-NSC through the dwarf-galaxy merger and the nuclear starburst it triggers. Panels (a.1) and (a.2) show the gas mass within $10\,\rm pc$ of BH-1 and BH-2, respectively, tracing the nuclear fuel reservoir available for accretion and nuclear star formation.
Panels (b.1) and (b.2) show the corresponding BH accretion rates (green) together with the Eddington-limited rate (grey dashed, rising as the BH mass grows, assuming a standard radiative efficiency of $\epsilon_{\rm r}=0.1$), and the star formation rate within $10\,\rm pc$ (grey shaded, right axis).
Panels (c.1) and (c.2) show the local SNe rate within $10\,\rm pc$ (purple) and the number of stars more massive than $8\,\rm M_{\odot}$ within $10\,\rm pc$ (grey, right axis). Outside the starburst phase, the local SNe regulate the local supply of gas by periodically ejecting gas and terminating the accretion cycles.
The galaxy-wide star formation rate is shown in panel (d), the global SNe rate in panel (e). The grey shading marks times after NSC coalescence ($t_{\rm coal}\sim 508\,\rm Myr$).
Gas capture by the NSCs and BHs is suppressed during the starburst and becomes episodic once the global SNe rate has decreased, after ${\sim}340\,\rm Myr$ (Section 3.3).

Figu$r$e 4: Dyn$a$mical evolution of the BH pair in the fiducial simulation (1e3-NSC, blue): The figure shows (a) pairwise separation r; (b) semi-major axis a once the BHs form a bound binary, with the triangle marking the merger; (c) eccentricity, shown as $1-e$; and (f) mass of each BH, which grows via gas accretion and through the merger at final time (the right-pointing triangle marker indicates the merger remnant mass).
Panel (d) shows the total hardening rate $s_{\rm total}$ as measured from the simulation, and its gravitational-wave contribution $s_{\rm GW}$ separately. The time at which gravitational waves take over is shown as a dashed vertical line (and a star marker in panel b).
The BBH-to-NSC mass ratio and the BH mass ratio $q=M_{2}/M_{1}\leq 1$ are shown in panel (e).
For comparison, we add the numerical experiment 1e3-NSC-reset (grey) in which the BH mass is instead reset to $10^{3}\,\rm M_{\odot}$ at $t\sim 460\,\rm Myr$ (Section 3.4).

Figure 5: Nuclear stellar and gas content within $r=1\,\rm pc$ of the BH binary in the fiducial simulation 1e3-NSC (blue), with the mass-reset numerical experiment of Figure 4, 1e3-NSC-reset, for comparison (grey): Panels (a.1) and (a.2) show the gas mass for both simulations, each showing repeated episodes of local gas capture and depletion (see the SNe regulation in Figure 3); (b) shows mass in newly-formed stars that depletes due to stellar scattering and stellar evolution mass-losses; (c) mass in old, pre-existing NSC stars. The NSC density drops due to BH binary scattering in the fiducial run, but is left essentially unperturbed by the much lighter BBH in 1e3-NSC-reset; (d) resulting mean total stellar mass density within $1\,\rm pc$, combining BBH scattering, star formation, and stellar-evolution mass loss. The vertical blue/grey lines mark the fiducial/reset binary’s coalescence time.

Figure 6: Mass ejec$t$ion rate from the nuclear star cluster in the fiducial simulation 1e3-NSC as a function of time. To qualify as an ejection, a star must be bound to the NSC at time t and unbound at $t+\Delta t$, with $\Delta t=7\,\rm Myr$, at a distance of more than $200\,\rm pc$ from the NSC. The mass ejection rate (panel a) peaks directly after the formation of the BH binary and then decays towards the BH merger, while the rate of kinetic energy carried away by the ejected stars (panel b) remains approximately constant.

Figure 7: Evolution of the distance of the NSCs to each other, the NSCs to their respective host galaxies (centre of the dark matter initially associated with each host galaxy), and the distance between NSCs and their BHs in simulation 1e3-NSC. The GW recoil leads to the ejection of the merger remnant from the nuclear star cluster, but it is retained inside the galaxy. The light and dark grey shaded regions mark the time after the coalescence of the NSCs and after the BH merger, respectively.

Figure 8: Evolution of the NSC during the galaxy merger, (a) before NSC coalescence, (b) after NSC coalescence but before hard binary formation, (c) during the BBH stellar scattering phase shortly before the merger, and (d) after the merger with BH recoil.
The first column shows the surface density of new stars over-plotted by the (old) NSC surface density (as in Figure 1). Columns two and three show the total surface density (old NSC + new stars), with contours of equal surface density in red. Column four shows individual stars in the $0.4\,\rm pc$ around the BH with NSC stars plotted in white, new stars in red, and massive new stars ($m>8\,\rm M_{\odot}$) in yellow. The locations of the BHs are shown as white and black dots, and the dashed cyan circles mark the sphere of influence $r_{\rm infl}$ of the BHs.
The NSC merger (b, $t=$508$\,\rm Myr$) adds mass to the outskirts of the NSC, such that the $10^{2}\,\rm M_{\odot}\,pc^{-2}$ contour moves to larger radii. During the scouring phase (508–$848\,\rm Myr$), the central density decreases and the $\Sigma=10^{4}\,\rm M_{\odot}\,pc^{-2}$ contour moves inwards. Ejected stars from the nuclear star cluster are visible as red dots scattered throughout the galaxy in the overview panels in rows (c) and (d). The BH merger recoil unbinds the NSC core on the scale of its sphere of influence ($r_{\rm infl}=3.96\,\rm pc$ before the ejection) and leaves behind a diffuse stellar core with surface density $\ll 10^{4}\,\rm M_{\odot}\,pc^{-2}$.

Figure 9: Evolution of the NSC. Panel (a) shows the evolution of the bound mass of the two NSCs and the contribution from new stars. New stars form episodically when gas becomes bound to the NSC (b). The size evolution of the NSC (half-mass radius $r_{1/2}$ and the BH sphere of influence $r_{\rm infl}$) is shown in (c). The distances between the NSCs, their host galaxies and their BHs are shown in Figure 7.

Figure 10: Histogram of the radial distribution of stellar mass that was last bound to one of the NSCs before NSC coalescence (a), during the NSC coalescence (b), and during the BH binary scattering phase (c). The plot hence indicates where stellar mass that was bound to the NSC at any time is re-distributed in the galaxy. $M_{\rm lost}$ is the mass that became unbound from either of the two NSCs during the respective period of time. During the NSC merger and the onset of BBH scattering, mass is distributed to kpc scales (via tidal stripping), but remains bound to the galaxy. During the BBH scattering phase, about 20 per cent of the cluster mass is lost, and ${\sim}2.5$ per cent of the NSC mass is ejected and becomes unbound from the galaxy.

2610.38767.abstract: Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) are expected to coexist in low-mass galaxies and might together facilitate the coalescence and growth of IMBHs. We simulate an equal-mass, gas-rich dwarf-galaxy merger in which each progenitor hosts a $10^3\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBH embedded in a $10^6\,\rm M_\odot$ NSC to study their co-evolution. The simulation model combines the multiphase interstellar medium and fully sampled initial stellar mass function of GRIFFIN at $4\,\rm M_\odot$ gas resolution with the regularised post-Newtonian black hole dynamics of KETJU. Black holes are modelled as accreting sink particles without feedback. Without NSCs, $10^3$-$10^4\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBHs sink only to separations of $50$-$200\,\rm pc$ and capture no gas. With NSCs, the clusters coalesce within ${\sim} 500\,\rm Myr$, the IMBHs form a binary within a few Myr, and scattering of mainly old NSC stars drives them to merger ${\sim} 340\,\rm Myr$ later. The NSCs also promote gas capture, growing the black holes to $1.1\times10^5$ and $4.1\times10^4\,\rm M_\odot$. Gas capture is suppressed during the merger-induced starburst by stellar feedback and the motion of the NSCs relative to the gas, and proceeds in brief supernova-regulated episodes once the NSCs have settled in the centre. Scattering by the IMBH binary and the merger recoil of ${\sim} 175\,\rm km\,s^{-1}$, which removes the remnant from the NSC but not from the galaxy, leave a larger, rotating NSC with a flat core. The stellar tidal disruption rate rises towards coalescence, and the merger is detectable with LISA out to high redshift. NSCs thus remove the delivery and hardening bottlenecks of IMBH mergers in low-mass galaxies.

2610.38779.abstract: Deep imaging surveys are revealing increasing numbers of low surface brightness stellar streams around Milky Way-like galaxies. These streams trace the orbital evolution and internal structure of their disrupted dwarf galaxy progenitors. We investigate the evolution and observability of tidal features from dwarf galaxies consistent with the $\Lambda$CDM framework and Local Group observations. We performed high-resolution $N$-body simulations of dwarf galaxies orbiting in a static Milky Way-like potential comprising a disc, bulge, and dark matter halo. Each dwarf comprised a Plummer stellar distribution embedded in a cuspy or cored generalised Navarro--Frenk--White dark matter halo. Idealised integrated surface brightness maps were constructed every 0.5 Gyr over 10 Gyr, and detectability was quantified through the projected area of stellar light brighter than limiting surface brightnesses, $\mu_{\rm lim}=29$--$32$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$, chosen to span depths relevant to ARRAKIHS, LSST, and Euclid. The detectability of tidal features depends most strongly on progenitor stellar mass, orbital configuration, parameterised by the eccentricity proxy $e_0$, and evolutionary stage. Across this range, extended tidal debris is predominantly recovered for initially more radial configurations, mainly those with $e_0 \gtrsim 0.75$. In the simulated grid, detectable area is dominated by $M_\star=10^8$--$10^9 M_\odot$ progenitors, whereas $M_\star=10^6$--$10^7 M_\odot$ systems can undergo stripping without detectable debris. The detectable area evolves non-monotonically with time, reflecting the competition between stream formation, phase mixing, and the fading of diffuse debris below the adopted surface brightness limits. Cuspy and cored progenitors show similar evolution of the detectable area, with differences smaller than the scatter induced by orbital diversity.

2610.38811.abstract: The Zone of Avoidance (ZoA) continues to represent the most significant incompleteness in the extragalactic census of the Local Universe. It is evident that photometric surveys alone are insufficient to establish whether the galaxy overdensities detected therein are physical systems or projections along the line of sight. We present the first spectroscopic results of the extragalactic science area of the KMOS VVVX-GalCen Spectroscopic Survey, demonstrating how near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy can reveal and dynamically characterise galaxy clusters hidden by the Milky Way. A photometric overdensity of 19 galaxy candidates was identified in the VVV NIRGC III catalogue, centred at $(l,b)=(274.05^\circ,+2.85^\circ)$ with a mean interstellar extinction of $A_{K_s}=0.2$ mag; 16 of these candidates were observed with VLT/KMOS in the $HK$ grating and yielded spectra with reliable cross-correlation radial velocities. A total of 14 galaxies form a compact structure with a mean redshift of $\langle z \rangle = 0.089 \pm 0.001$, which corresponds to a mean radial velocity $\langle cz \rangle = 26660 \pm 170$ km/s, while two are foreground galaxies. The rest-frame line-of-sight velocity dispersion is $\sigma_v = 560^{+110}_{-120}$ km/s, implying an indicative dynamical mass of $M_{200} = 1.9^{+0.7}_{-1.1} \times 10^{14} M_\odot$ (based on members within the cluster core $\sim 0.4 r_{200}$) and placing the system in the poor-cluster regime. Of these 14 cluster members, 13 also lie within the $2\sigma$ scatter of the fitted near-IR red sequence. The other two galaxies are foreground objects that lie outside this range.

2610.38836.abstract: While numerous studies have shown that satellite galaxies experience declining star formation rates after infall, direct comparisons across different surveys and redshifts are complicated by varying sample selections, environmental metrics, and techniques used to derive galaxy properties. In this work, we select satellite galaxies from the highly complete Galaxy and Mass Assembly (GAMA) Survey and the Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS) to investigate environmental quenching out to z~0.4. These surveys derive galaxy properties and environments in a consistent manner, minimizing systematic biases and enabling a robust comparison across redshift. Using projected phase space as a proxy for infall time, we quantify the evolution of the quenched fraction and trace how satellites evolve relative to the star-forming main sequence (SFMS). We find consistent trends between GAMA and DEVILS, with satellites exhibiting a steady decline in star formation relative to the SFMS at a rate of ~0.14 dex/Gyr following infall. Extending this analysis to include visual morphology, we find similar declining trends for both early- and late-type systems. Overall, we find no significant redshift evolution between GAMA and DEVILS, indicating that group and cluster environments have a comparable impact on the star formation activity of satellite galaxies over the past ~4.5 Gyr.

2610.38886.title: Odds Estimation for Supermassive Black Hole Binaries in Local Core Galaxies

figures.caption: Figure 1: The purple solid curve shows the local galaxy stellar mass function used to down-sample the catalog of IllustrisTNG subhalos used in our core-formation model. It is described by a single Schechter function whose normalization, amplitude, and index controlling the sharpness of the transition from low- to high-mass are selected to be consistent with the nanohertz gravitational-wave background. The pink shaded region depicts the 16% and 84% confidence regions. The black data points with error bars show the mean core galaxy stellar mass function (above $10^{10}M_{\odot}$) produced by our model across 1000 iterations.

Figure 2: We show the feature space distributions according to single (blue) or binary (orange) occupation. The histograms show the binned posteriors, while the smooth curves are kernel density estimations. The shaded region shows the 16% and 84% confidence region. Colored points represent the eight model-selected candidates described in section V.1. The feature distributions are well separated, indicating that they are informative for the logistic classifier. The lack of significant covariance between features reflects low variance-inflation factors and allows the derived regression coefficients to be interpreted physically.

Figure 3: We show the logistic regression coefficient posteriors for 1000 iterations of our core-scouring model. The distributions are well constrained, capturing robust information about host properties that result in surviving binaries. The histograms show the binned posteriors, while the smooth curves are kernel density estimations. The shaded region shows the 16% and 84% confidence region, while the dashed lines show the maximum-likelihood estimate for each coefficient. The 2D histograms show the covariances for each coefficient, which appear as expected for low variance-inflation factors among the features. We find the maximum likelihood values of the coefficients to be ${\cal A}=-2.17,\ {\cal B}=-2.54,\ {\cal C}=1.80,$ and ${\cal D}=-3.77$.

Figure 4: The predicted separation distribution for dual (pink) and binary (orange) SMBHs in local core galaxies. The histograms show the binned $z=0$ separations of each black hole pair across 1000 iterations of our core-scouring model. The smooth curves are kernel density estimations. The shaded regions show the 16% and 84% intervals and the dashed lines show the maximum-likelihood estimates. Duals in the model tend to cluster around the initial separation, pointing to low stellar densities and inefficient dynamical friction in the host galaxies. Binary separations peak at subparsec distances. At larger separations ($\sim 10^{1}$–$10^{3}$ pc) hardening is efficient and pairs spend little time in this regime.

Figure 5: The distributions of total black hole mass, mass ratio, and present-day separation for binaries across all model realizations (orange) alongside distributions of black hole mass and mass ratio for single SMBHs at $z=0$ (blue). Histograms show the binned data while smooth curves are kernel density estimations. The dashed lines show the maximum-likelihood estimates while shaded regions show the 16 and 84 percentiles. Surviving binaries tend to have higher total mass and lower mass ratio than those which have coalesced, reflecting assembly via hierarchical merging. Present-day binaries with higher total mass tend to exist at larger separations.

Figure 6: The histogram shows the posterior distribution of circular gravitational wave frequencies of surviving binaries across all model outputs. The smooth curve is a kernel density estimate with the purple shaded region indicating the 16 to 84 percentile range. The dashed line shows the most likely frequency ($2.1\times 10^{-10}\ {\rm Hz}$). The pink shaded region shows the frequency space pulsar timing arrays are sensitive to. Only a small portion of all $z=0$ binaries in the model (0.3%) are active as pulsar timing array sources. Most binaries are either too widely separated or else have already evolved past the relevant regime.

Figure 7: Comparison of the feature distributions for both the observed sample of core galaxies (pink) and all cores formed in our models (purple). Histograms show the binned parameters while smooth curves are kernel density estimations. Shaded regions are the 16 and 84 percentile ranges and dashed lines show the maximum likelihood feature values. The observed and simulated distributions are broadly consistent–a manifestation of the mass fundamental plane and the fact the core model used in the analysis was calibrated to the mass deficits of the observed sample. Of note, however, is the tendency of the observed sample toward more diffuse systems. This is caused by the over-representation of BCGs in the observed catalog of cores. We also point out that the variance in the mass deficit at each stellar mass is much higher in the observed sample than in the model population. We discuss potential reasons for this in section V.3.

2610.38886.abstract: Supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs) are expected products of massive galaxy mergers, but identifying binaries in nearby galaxies remains challenging. We combine simulated massive-galaxy assembly histories from IllustrisTNG with a semi-analytic core-scouring model to connect observable core galaxy properties to the probability of hosting a bound SMBHB at z=0. We (i) construct a core galaxy population using an observationally motivated galaxy stellar mass function, (ii) model binary evolution through dynamical friction, stellar hardening, and gravitational-wave emission, and (iii) perform logistic regressions with five observable predictors: stellar mass deficit, stellar mass, central density, central velocity dispersion, and effective radius. The resulting models perform well on simulated systems, achieving a pseudo-$R^2$ of $0.51\pm0.03$, accuracy $0.95\pm0.01$, precision $0.92\pm0.03$, and recall $0.82\pm0.04$. Uncoalesced binaries are typically compact, with separations peaking near 0.3 pc, though only $\sim0.3\%$ emit in the pulsar timing array band. Applying the model to observed core galaxies, we identify eight nearby galaxies more likely than not to host SMBHBs. Of those eight host candidates, we note Messier 86 (NGC 4406) as a particularly likely example that was similarly identified using independent means and therefore warrants future follow-up.

2610.38923.abstract: A variety of faint and observationally challenging stellar systems has been discovered in the Milky Way in the last decades. Unveiling their kinematic and chemical properties is crucial to understand their nature and to assess their role in the history of our Galaxy. In this paper, we present a chemo-dynamical analysis of four elusive stellar systems (BH 140, Garro 01, BLISS 1, and Kim 3) using spectra collected with the X-shooter medium-resolution spectrograph at the VLT. We derived precise line-of-sight velocities and chemical abundances for all targets. Specifically, we provide the first spectroscopic characterization of metallicity and {\alpha}-element content for BH 140, the first comprehensive chemical characterization for BLISS 1 and Garro 01, and the first spectroscopic metallicity determination for Kim 3. BH 140, Garro 01 and BLISS 1 are relatively metal-rich systems with [Fe/H] ~ -0.7 dex and have enhanced {\alpha}-element abundances, whereas Kim 3 is notably metal-poor with [Fe/H] ~ -1.8 dex. We also performed an orbital analysis to investigate their origin as accreted or in situ systems. We found that Garro 01 and BH 140 have orbits confined within < 1.5 kpc from the Galactic plane, the former having also a remarkably circular orbit. They were likely born in situ, although the high orbital eccentricity of BH 140 and its mild deficiency in {\alpha}-elements leave other possibilities open. Although undoubtedly accreted, BLISS 1 does not exhibit a clear dynamical association with any known progenitor, lying in a high energy (E) - high vertical angular momentum (LZ ) prograde orbit reaching a maximum height from the Galactic plane of zmax ~ 8 kpc. Its chemical properties seem to favor an in situ origin, which might be connected with the Aleph sub-structure. Finally, we tentatively link the high energy and low LZ orbit of Kim 3 to the Elqui stream.

Figure 2: A Loomis-Wood plot of the $K_{a}=0$ a-type transitions of 3-methoxypropanol in the 150–170 GHz range. In this format, the actual frequencies of the selected transitions are easily identified in the six peaks in the right half of the plot that align in a nearly linear pattern. This linear patterns arises from the simulated transition frequencies steadily becoming more inaccurate due to errors in the rotational parameters as the $J$ levels of the transition increase.

Figure 4: The relative energies of the five isomers of methoxypropanol, computed by the AIMNet2 neural network model [21]. Each isomer is depicted in its most stable geometry. In most isomers, there is some stabilizing interaction between the -OH group and a lone pair of electrons in the -OCH3 group. In 3-methoxypropanol, the groups are far enough apart that a pseudo six membered ring can form via an intramolecular hydrogen bond. This noncovalent hydrogen bond is indicated with a dashed line.

2610.38934.abstract: The methoxy functionalized alcohol species methoxymethanol and 2-methoxyethanol have recently been identified toward the MM1 protostellar source in the NGC 6334I massive star-forming region. Here we report measurements of portions of the centimeter, millimeter, and sub-millimeter regions of the rotational spectrum of the most stable conformer of 3-methoxy-1-propanol in order to probe the presence of even larger methoxylated alcohols toward the source. The experimental rotational parameters determined from these spectra were used to simulate the rotational spectrum of 3-methoxy-1-propanol under the physical conditions of the MM1 source and compared to the same ALMA observational dataset of the source in which 2-methoxyethanol was first discovered. No 3-methoxy-1-propanol transitions are identified in the data, and an upper limit on its column density toward the source was determined to be $7.5 \cdot 10^{15} \text{ cm}^{-2}$. When considering the series of these three methoxy alcohols, the decrease in column density going from 2-methoxyethanol to 3-methoxy-1-propanol is consistent with how the column density of 2-methoxyethanol decreases compared to methoxymethanol.
